title: What an award show is
description:
An award show is a ceremony where a voting body honors the year's outstanding work in a field — film, music, television, theatre. The format is ritual: nominations build suspense, the ceremony delivers verdicts, and the winners' speeches become cultural text. Award shows matter because they convert taste into history — the winners list becomes the canon.

The major American shows form an ecosystem: the Oscars (film), Grammys (music), Emmys (television), and Tonys (theatre). Film festivals (Cannes, Berlin, Venice, Sundance) and industry awards (BAFTA, Golden Globes, CMA, Billboard) complete the calendar. Each has its own voters, rules, and prestige economy.

title: EGOT: the grand slam
description:
EGOT — Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, Tony — is the rarest achievement in entertainment. Completing it requires mastery across television, music, film, and theatre, usually over decades. Richard Rodgers was the first to complete it (1962); Robert Lopez the youngest and fastest (10 years); Viola Davis the most recent (2023, Grammy for her memoir).

The EGOT's prestige comes from its cross-disciplinary demand: almost no career naturally spans all four. Honorary or non-competitive awards don't count in the strict definition — only competitive wins.

title: The Big Four
description:
The Oscars (1929), Grammys (1959), Emmys (1949), and Tonys (1947) are the four pillars of American entertainment awards. Each is voted by its industry's professionals; each has a signature trophy (Oscar, gramophone, winged Emmy, medallion); each anchors its field's calendar.

Together they define the awards season from winter to spring: Globes and Grammys in winter, Oscars in March, Tonys in June, Emmys in September.

title: Awards season calendar
description:
Awards season runs roughly November to June: critics' prizes in December, Golden Globes in January, Grammys in February, BAFTAs in February, the Oscars in March, Pulitzers in April, Cannes in May, and the Tonys in June. Campaigns — screenings, ads, interviews — run the whole way.

The calendar's order matters: early wins build momentum ('precursors'), and each body's different voters can crown different champions.

title: How Oscar voting works
description:
About 10,000 Academy members vote: branches nominate within their crafts (actors nominate actors), then the full membership votes winners in most categories. Best Picture uses a preferential (ranked) ballot since 2009, rewarding the film with the broadest support.

Campaigning is regulated but intense: screeners, Q&As, and 'for your consideration' ads flood the season.

title: A short history of award shows
t: A short history of award shows
description:
The Oscars (1929) invented the form: a private banquet that became, with 1953's first telecast, a national ritual. The Tonys (1947), Emmys (1949), and Grammys (1959) followed, each adapting the template to its medium. Television made stars of the ceremonies themselves — hosts, speeches, and upsets became programming.

The modern era added precursors, campaigns, and the internet's instant verdicts. Through it all, the core transaction endures: a profession telling the world what it values.

title: Famous acceptance moments
description:
Award shows live in their unscripted minutes: Marlon Brando sending Sacheen Littlefeather to decline his Oscar (1973), the Moonlight/La La Land envelope correction (2017), Kanye West interrupting Taylor Swift at the VMAs (2009), and countless speeches that outlived the night.

The best speeches share a structure: surprise, gratitude, and one true sentence. The worst are lists of agents.

description: The In Memoriam segment — the year's departed honored in montage — is awards television's most solemn ritual. Omissions spark annual outrage; inclusions spark debate about who counts. Done well, it reminds the room that the art outlives the artists.

title: The hosts
description:
Hosting is the hardest job in show business: three-plus hours of live television, a divided room, and a global audience. The greats — Bob Hope (19 Oscars), Billy Crystal (9), Johnny Carson (5), Whoopi Goldberg, Chris Rock — combined monologue craft with room command.

Recent years have experimented with no host at all, trading monologue risk for pace.

title: Ratings: the audience story
description:
Award-show ratings peaked in the late 1990s (Titanic's Oscars drew 57+ million Americans) and declined through the streaming era as viewing fragmented. Ceremonies responded with shorter runtimes, popular-film categories, and hostless experiments.

The decline mirrors television's: the monoculture that made award shows mass events has dissolved into niches.

title: The precursor circuit
description:
Before the big nights come the precursors: critics' prizes (New York, LA, National Society), guild awards (DGA, PGA, SAG, WGA), and the Globes/BAFTAs. Each has different voters and predictive power — the DGA predicts the Oscar director race well; critics often diverge.

Campaigns treat precursors as primaries: wins build the narrative of inevitability.

title: How Golden Globe voting worked
description:
The Hollywood Foreign Press Association — under 100 international journalists at its peak — voted the Golden Globes from 1944 to 2023, across film and television. After ethics and diversity controversies, the HFPA dissolved in 2023 and a new, larger international voting body took over.

The Globes' small electorate made them the most idiosyncratic major awards — and the most fun to predict.

description:

BAFTA's Outstanding British Film prize guarantees homegrown cinema its own spotlight.

title: How the Nobel Prizes are decided
t: How the Nobel Prizes are decided
description:
Four institutions decide: the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences (Physics, Chemistry, Economics), Karolinska Institutet (Medicine), the Swedish Academy (Literature), and the Norwegian Nobel Committee (Peace). Nominations are sealed for 50 years; campaigning disqualifies.

The December 10 ceremony — Nobel's death anniversary — closes the year in Stockholm and Oslo.

title: How the Pulitzer Prizes are decided
t: How the Pulitzer Prizes are decided
description:
Expert juries narrow thousands of entries to three finalists per category; the 19-member Pulitzer Board at Columbia University picks winners each April — and may overrule juries, as it famously did in 1941.

Fifteen journalism prizes plus books, drama, and music make 23 categories.

t: Cannes juries: how the Palme is chosen
description:

Legendary presidents — from Tennessee Williams to Greta Gerwig — shaped cinema history from the jury room.

t: Fan-voted awards: People's Choice and the VMAs
description:

Studios campaign for fan wins because they signal genuine audience love.

description:

The play-off music is itself a ritual — and occasionally a controversy.
